title: Encore AI raises $30M to build AI agents that learn from customer calls
teaser: Encore AI’s new agents learn more than data—they adopt the specific jokes and playbooks from successful human customer calls.
summary: Encore AI raised $30 million in a Series A round to expand its AI platform. The company specializes in deploying advanced voice agents that learn optimal customer interaction tactics through a process called "interaction mining." This system analyzes vast amounts of data—including call recordings, emails, and texts—to identify the most successful 'playbooks' used by human employees. These agents then replicate these specific conversational patterns (like jokes or anecdotes) to optimize sales and support processes. Already serving over 40 enterprise clients, primarily financial institutions, Encore plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. presence.
author: Ram Iyer
content: Encore AI , a startup that studies companies' customer interactions to train and deploy AI voice agents that can work alongside customer support and sales teams, or operate autonomously, has raised $30 million in a Series A round led by Team8. Founded in 2022 as Insait IO by CEO Dvir Ginzburg, the company started out building recommendation software for financial advisers and relationship managers. Now rebranded as Encore AI, the startup has expanded that system into a platform that analyzes conversations between a company's employees and customers to identify which approaches resulted in successful outcomes, and uses those findings to train its AI agents. The result, according to Ginzburg, is an AI agent that leverages the strongest parts of the playbooks used by an organization's employees. "Sometimes our agents even tell the jokes that the relationship managers are telling, or give the anecdotes or examples that the relationship managers are giving, because we literally run by the playbooks that we see working [...] The agent we build is a package of many different playbooks that have worked throughout the process," he told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. Ginzburg calls the process "interaction mining." The company's platform collects call recordings, emails, and text messages, and connects that info with CRM systems. It then divides the customer interactions into stages and tries to find out which parts of a conversation helped move the process along, and which failed. This lets Encore's agents, and consequently its customers, learn what works best for any particular client or interaction, as different employees may be either more or less effective at different points during a sales or customer success process, Ginzburg told TechCrunch. The company's platform also lets companies identify where their existing customer support and sales processes are falling short, identify inefficiencies and friction points, and find key issues. A screenshot of Encore AI's interaction mining tool Image Credits: Encore AI Encore says its agents can communicate directly with customers by voice or text, as well as act as assistants to employees, recommending responses and tactics during conversations. The company has more than 40 enterprise customers globally, the majority of which are financial institutions, according to Ginzburg. He said Encore's annual recurring revenue has increased more than 5x since it raised its seed round less than 18 months ago, though he declined to disclose exact revenue numbers or valuation. Encore's early to this market, but its share may become harder to defend as large CRM providers like Salesforce, SAP, Zoho, and HubSpot can build similar AI capabilities around their customers' data. But Ginzburg contends that access to data alone isn't enough, as established vendors would need to overhaul their processes to make historical customer conversations the foundation of their agents like Encore does. "The biggest players that we are competing against, they don't see [conversational] history as a data point that they are utilizing. For them to start asking for conversational data with their current employees will require changing their entire implementation stack and technological stack," he said. Planven, Lukatz, and Garage also participated in the round, as did some banks and insurers. Encore said some of the financial institutions participating in the round first used its product before deciding to invest. The startup plans to use proceeds from the Series A to expand its U.S. sales operations and deploy its platform with more large financial institutions.

title: Elon Musk’s X settles multiyear legal battle with the World Federation of Advertisers
teaser: After a multiyear legal battle, Elon Musk's X settles with the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA), ending claims that advertisers illegally boycotted the platform over brand safety issues.
summary: Elon Musk’s social network, X, has settled its long-standing legal dispute with the advertising trade group WFA. The settlement puts past litigation involving the Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM) behind both parties. X had accused WFA of orchestrating a 'systematic illegal boycott' after Musk's 2022 takeover, alleging advertisers pulled spending due to brand safety concerns. Advertisers countered that brands should have autonomy in ad spending. Previously, a federal court dismissed X's lawsuit for failing to prove harm. Following the settlement, WFA announced it has discontinued GARM and affirmed its commitment to free speech, resetting the contentious relationship between the two organizations.
author: Aisha Malik
content: Elon Musk's X has settled its multiyear legal battle with advertising trade group the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA), the two organizations said on Wednesday. The settlement ends Musk's aggressive attempt to hold advertisers legally responsible for pulling spending from X over brand safety concerns. X sued the WFA in 2024 for conducting what it called a "systematic illegal boycott" of the platform after it saw a decline in advertising revenue following Musk's $44 billion takeover of the social network in 2022. Companies X accused of doing so included Mars, CVS Health, Shell, Lego, and more. The advertisers rejected the allegations and argued that brands are free to decide where to spend their advertising dollars. A federal court dismissed the lawsuit in March after a judge said X had failed to demonstrate that it had suffered any harm under federal competition laws. X had appealed the decision in April. "Today the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA) and X Corp. are putting the litigation involving the Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM) behind them," the joint statement reads. "This resets the relationship between the two organizations." X had alleged that advertisers reduced their spending because of guidelines developed by the WFA's Global Alliance for Responsible Media, a coalition of brands and advertising agencies that was established to develop standards aimed at preventing ads from being displayed alongside harmful online ⁠content. Advertisers were concerned that their brands would appear alongside harmful content on the social network after Musk overhauled the platform's content moderation policies. "WFA reiterates its commitment to freedom of speech, a principle first included in WFA's founding constitution back in 1953, and a principle it shares with X," the statement reads. "On August 9, 2024, WFA discontinued GARM. WFA will not form or restart GARM or a similar initiative. WFA and X are fully aligned in the view that brands, platforms, and consumers will all benefit from brand-safety innovation." The lawsuit wasn't the only time Musk clashed with advertisers. After acquiring X, he told advertisers who paused spending on the platform to "go f*** yourself."

title: Full school day cellphone bans are more popular than ever
teaser: Support for full school day cellphone bans is soaring, reaching 48% of US adults—a significant jump from just 36% two years ago.
summary: A new Pew Research Center survey indicates strong, increasing national support for banning cellphones in schools. Seventy-seven percent of US adults back a ban in middle and high school classes, with 48% supporting an all-day ('bell-to-bell') restriction. This represents a sharp increase from the 36% support seen two years ago. Support is broadly bipartisan (Republicans: 55%; Democrats: 44%), and over 20 states have already adopted these bans. Research suggests mixed effects: some studies note positive student well-being outcomes and fewer unexcused absences, while others show no direct impact on test scores.
author: Lauren Feiner
content: As schools across the country continue to implement cellphone bans, a new Pew Research Center survey shows they continue to gain support. Seventy-seven percent of US adults support banning cellphones in middle and high school classes, and 48 percent support banning them for the entire school day. That's the first time more Americans have supported, rather than opposed, so-called bell-to-bell bans. Two years ago, just 36 percent of American adults supported an all day ban. Across all age groups over 18 that were surveyed, most respondents support in-class bans. That support is lower but still at least half for all-day bans across most age groups, except for ages 18-29, where support for a bell-to-bell ban drops to just 28 percent. Republicans were slightly more likely to favor both in-class and all-day bans, at 81 percent and 55 percent, respectively. But Democrats were also broadly supportive of in-class bans at 74 percent, and all-day bans at 44 percent. More than 20 states havre already adopted bell-to-bell cellphone bans , and early studies show mixed impacts. One report found positive long-term effects on students' well-being, but no evidence of an impact on test scores. Another found higher suspension rates in the first year of a ban, that later returned to normal levels, and a decrease in unexcused absences.

title: Google brings its age-assurance technology to Android developers worldwide
teaser: Google is rolling out a new 'Play Signal API' that lets developers screen apps for appropriate content by reading an opt-in age range, enhancing child safety globally.
summary: To enhance child safety, Google announced it is rolling out its Play Signal API, an age-assurance technology for Android developers globally by the end of 2026. This tool allows developers to provide safer, age-appropriate experiences by identifying a user's general age range without accessing sensitive personal data like date of birth. Initially expanding to Australia and Canada by mid-August, the feature centralizes parental controls within Family Link. Crucially, sharing this information is opt-in, requiring parents to actively enter their child’s age range. This development aligns with global regulatory pressure (like Apple's tools) to better protect minors in app ecosystems.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Google is expanding its answer to Apple's age-assurance tools with Wednesday's news that it will bring its Play Signal API to users worldwide by the end of 2026. The technology, already available in Brazil, allows Android developers to identify younger users of their apps in order to provide safer, age-appropriate experiences. The expansion will initially bring the API to Australia and Canada by mid-August, before rolling out globally to all markets by the end of the year. Its arrival comes as lawmakers and regulators around the world are increasingly pressuring app stores to provide better protections for minors. Apple, for instance, launched its age-verification tools globally in February to comply with the growing number of age-verification laws. Image Credits: Google Like Apple, Google's technology allows developers to obtain a user's age range without needing to access personal information, like their date of birth. Instead, it enables parents to share their child's age range directly with apps. It also lets adults share their age when prompted by app developers as well, allowing for customized experiences. Parents won't have to manage sharing this information on an app-by-app basis, either. To make it easier, Google centralizes these controls inside its parental controls dashboard, Family Link . Once entered, any developer that chooses to incorporate age-range information can access this signal to customize their apps accordingly. Google notes, however, that the age ranges are not shared by default - parents must opt in by entering that information. The feature joins other safety tools on Google Play, including those that let developers restrict a child's ability to discover their apps. Parents, meanwhile, can continue to use Google Play's Family Link app to manage their child's screen-time limits, approve app downloads, or set PIN-based content filters for specific apps.

title: Sorry, haters. Ferrari’s first EV is doing just fine
teaser: Despite initial hate, Ferrari's polarizing debut EV, the Luce, hit its sales target fast, showing strong demand from China.
summary: Against initial critical backlash and predictions of failure, Ferrari's first electric vehicle (EV), the Luce, has exceeded expectations. Initially criticized for its polarizing design, the car was largely designed by Jony Ive/LoveFrom. Despite early setbacks, sales reports indicate that Ferrari reached its projected target for the Luce quickly. This success is reportedly fueled by strong demand from China and wealthy buyers in tech hubs like Silicon Valley. Priced around €555,000, the company plans to sell approximately 2,500 units by 2030, marking a significant pivot into the EV market.
author: Tim De Chant
content: Sometimes the crowd isn't so wise. When Ferrari revealed the Luce - its first EV - to the public in May, the internet reacted. And not in a positive way. Critics compared the wedge-shaped Luce with a Nissan Leaf and said Chinese EVs would outperform it while undercutting it on price. Even former Ferrari chair Luca Cordero di Montezemolo was among the haters. Ferrari's stock dropped 8% the day after the reveal. Their conclusion: the Luce would be a dud. It turns out, the armchair auto executives were wrong about the five-seater that was largely designed by Jony Ive and his firm, LoveFrom. Ferrari hit this year's sales target for the Luce in just two months, according to a report by the Financial Times. The automaker was hoping to sell just under 500 of the €555,000 EVs ($630,000), and based on previous reports , it sounds like at least 20% will make their way to China. That's not surprising, given that the Luce seems tailor-made for the Chinese market , which favors fast, sleek four-door EVs. TechCrunch has reached out to Ferrari to confirm the figures, and we'll update this article if we receive a reply. Much of the internet's hate was directed at the Luce's styling, which hewed to some Ferrari norms while throwing others out the window. Appearance is subjective, and I've seen enough cars in my day to know that some designs don't translate well on screen. Maybe seeing one in person tipped buyers into placing an order. What's more, Ferrari has an enthusiastic and price-insensitive customer base. The company sold more than 13,000 cars last year, which is a lot for an automaker that specializes in six-figure vehicles. Ferrari buyers tend to own several models, so it's also not difficult to imagine 500 of them wanting a practical vehicle that's also a Ferrari. Is the Luce worth the price of admission? Early reviews suggest that it drives like a Ferrari should. Plus, it has the prancing horse on the hood. That appears to be all Ferrari needs to succeed.

title: The US government just banned Roombas
teaser: The new robot ban is far broader than humanoids: it threatens vacuum cleaners and delivery bots if they aren't built using US components.
summary: The FCC is banning new imports of 'advanced robotic devices,' citing national security risks linked primarily to foreign (especially Chinese) manufacturing. While headlines focused on humanoid robots, the ban's definition is much broader: it covers any ground-traveling, wireless robot weighing over 4.4 pounds—encompassing vacuum cleaners and delivery bots alike. The policy effectively impacts most roborobotic companies because top players are largely China-based. Companies seeking waivers must commit to local US manufacturing processes and design. Crucially, the FCC confirmed that existing devices already in use, such as current Roombas or routers, remain unaffected by the ban.
author: Sean Hollister
content: When the Trump administration announced yesterday that it was banning "advanced robotic devices" from entering the United States , the headlines were all about humanoids . But spying doesn't require legs - and neither does the FCC's robot ban. The robot ban will sweep up robot vacuum cleaners too , FCC media relations director Katie Gorscak confirms to The Verge. It's not coming for your existing Roomba, and companies can keep importing and selling already approved ones. But the government claims that future foreign robots pose a national security risk, and even robovac companies are suddenly being asked to commit to US manufacturing. While the government did include "humanoid robots" and "quadrupeds" among the bots it wants to ban, the ban is far broader than that. It covers almost any new software-controlled robot that travels over the ground, weighs more than 4.4 pounds (including any dock), can perceive its environment, and has wireless connectivity. By that definition, the FCC is banning future robot lawnmowers, sidewalk delivery robots, and the robots that crate around packages at your local Amazon warehouse. How the government defines the "advanced robotic devices" that will be banned from import. Image: FCC It was already clear from the government's ban announcement that it was thinking about robot vacuums. In the National Security Determination that the FCC is using to justify the ban, the government explicitly calls out my reporting on the incredibly poor security that let one man access 7,000 DJI robovacs around the world . But like the consumer router ban , the FCC isn't actually targeting companies with poor security. It's targeting basically every robovac company, regardless of their security practices - because basically every robovac is manufactured outside the US. The FCC is literally demonizing human and dog-shaped robots in this image tweeted by chair Brendan Carr. But that's the tip of the iceberg. Image: FCC Even before the US-based maker of the Roomba went bankrupt , its robots were built by a Chinese company. Just like Apple and Google and most every other gadget brand, these things are not produced domestically. Today, the vast majority of robot vacuums are designed by Chinese companies, too - all of the top five, including Roborock, Ecovacs, Dreame, Xiaomi, and Narwal, are Chinese entities. Even Dyson is turning to Chinese manufacturers . Following bankruptcy, the Roomba brand is now owned by its former China-based contract manufacturer Picea . "There are very few non-Chinese brands these days and their share is so small that it's difficult to track," IDC analyst Jitesh Ubrani tells The Verge . Even Matic, our top robovac pick that's assembled in California, may have to apply for a waiver for new models. It doesn't yet source 65 percent of components from the United States, co-founder and CEO Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge . Because yes, even US companies need to swear their robots are made in the US to get the government's waiver. Meanwhile, foreign companies will need to swear they're investing in US manufacturing - or lie, like that DJI front company I wrote about . If Trump and Carr were focused on actually protecting US citizens from the incredibly worrying security practices of smart home companies, I might argue that the FCC shouldn't exempt cleaning robots, as they can spy just as effectively as a humanoid. The DJI Romo robovac was a chilling example, letting someone on the other side of the planet map out my colleague Thomas Ricker's home , but it gets much worse - read about the robot lawnmower that ran me over to hear how. But again, the government isn't asking these companies any questions about security - not one - to get the waiver that lets them through. The FCC only wants to know where they're designed and made and assembled and tested and influenced, and get a specific commitment to start manufacturing them in the US instead. Even then, it appears the FCC will simply preference US companies without any new commitments to security or US manufacturing, like it did when it almost immediately let Netgear off the hook - even though Netgear's routers were among those targeted in the Volt Typhoon incident that helped justify the router ban to begin with. Four unnamed sources told Reuters that "the FCC is expected to exempt many non-Chinese suppliers from the restrictions." The government isn't de facto banning every type of robot made outside the US without its special waiver. It already has exceptions for self-driving cars and trains, unmanned aircraft and underwater vehicles, surgical robots, wheelchairs, and fixed robot arms for industrial and medical use. But most robots now have an uncertain future in the United States. It's also worth repeating that the FCC is not coming for your existing robots, just like it isn't coming for your existing routers or drones. But it's also worth repeating that if these gadgets truly pose a national security risk, it's kind of silly to do nothing about the ones we've already purchased. title: The Nothing Ear 3A look great… and sound good enough
teaser: The Nothing Ear 3A earbuds offer robust audio customization for just $99, despite minor flaws in ANC stability and call clarity.
summary: Reviewing the Nothing Ear 3A earbuds, the author highlights their transparent design and impressive value at $99. While the default sound is overly bass-heavy, the extensive parametric EQ (with four presets and an advanced 3-band/8-band options) allows for deep customization, significantly improving audio balance. Performance features include support for high-res LDAC codec and improved ANC, which filters out low drones effectively. However, the review notes minor performance flaws: adaptive ANC can exhibit sudden, disorienting intensity adjustments, and call quality is unreliable in noisy environments (e.g., sounding 'dark' when ambient noise increases). Despite these issues, the overall value—especially with enhanced controls via the Nothing X app—makes them highly recommended for their price point.
author: John.Higgins
content: Nothing has had a strong visual identity since the Ear 1 were released in 2021 for $99 and challenged the notion that a highly featured headset requires a high price. The Ear 3A have the same transparent look as Nothing's previous earbuds, with a clear case and stem design accented by a solid-colored body - this time adding a striking pink alongside yellow, black, and white options. And Nothing continues to improve both ANC and audio performance. But the Ear 3A also share the buggy performance that has plagued Nothing earbuds. While $99 is an attractive price for them, be ready to deal with some minor adaptive ANC and call quality issues. $99 The Good Great overall performance for the price Robust EQ The Bad Default sound is bass-heavy Some inconsistencies with adaptive ANC The Ear 3A have 12mm dynamic drivers and support the high-res LDAC codec, along with SBC and AAC. Their default sound is very heavy on the bass, and while it gives bass lines extra punch, the midrange - which includes vocals and guitars - gets covered by the excessive low end. Bassheads might enjoy it, but it's far too much for my taste, and I expect that will be the same for most people. Where I might ding some points for this on other earbuds, the Nothing 3A save themselves from that because of the robust EQ in the app. There's a simple interface with four presets and a custom 3-band EQ, a nice 8-band parametric EQ that gives you more advanced adjustments, and some additional EQ profiles from users curated by Nothing. In less than a minute I was able to adjust the EQ to something far more balanced to my ear (I added a downward slope to the bass below 115Hz, mid boost between 220-540Hz, another slight cut to the shouty frequencies between 2-3.5kHz, and some extra highs above 6.6kHz for a more open sound). It gave Chris Robinson's voice more presence on "Thorn in My Pride" and his brother Rich and Marc Ford's guitars nice crunch and bite as the song builds through the solo. And even with the cut to the low end, Johnny Colt's bass supports the band throughout. Nothing added a pink color to go along with yellow, white, and black options. ANC performance is improved over previous Nothing earbuds, with solid cancellation particularly in the lower mids and bass range, so low drones like air conditioners or plane cabin noise get filtered out very well. For $99, they also do a decent job with higher frequencies, but if you plan to use them consistently in a coffee shop you'll still hear orders being called out a bit. And if the high ANC setting is too much for you, there are mid and low settings that let in a bit more of the low end to ground you in reality. There's also an adaptive ANC setting, but here's where some of the minor issues I encountered started. While out on walks around the neighborhood, occasionally (maybe two or three times during an hour walk) the ANC intensity would quickly adjust to let in much more ambient noise and then switch back to its previous level. The whole experience lasted maybe two seconds each time and was disorienting. I tried to take note of what might have triggered it, but couldn't find a consistent situation that would cause it to happen. In general, whenever the adaptive ANC makes a change to the intensity, it's sudden instead of the more gradual change that my Apple AirPods Pro 3 or Sony WF-1000XM6 do - for hundreds of dollars more. The one issue I was able to figure out, also about volume attenuation, was with my call quality. While talking to a friend I regularly call when testing earbuds, if I was just listening to him, he couldn't hear anything from my side at all. No traffic, no wind, no breathing, nothing. At one point he wondered aloud if the call had disconnected. When I was talking, I sounded clear and natural to him if I started talking when there wasn't a lot of ambient noise around me. When the sound around me got louder - such as more cars driving by - a bit of that sound leaked through, although my voice still sounded natural. But if I started talking while there was a lot of noise around me, my voice sounded dark as the earbuds strongly filtered out upper-mid and high frequencies, including doing a great job tamping down the loud ambient sound. The Ear 3A have the same transparent design Nothing has used since the introduction of the Ear 1 in 2021. The Nothing X app includes controls for ANC intensity, a great parametric EQ, and customized controls. Both the ANC and call quality issues could be addressed with future firmware updates (my testing was with firmware 1.0.1.59), and if you use one of the static ANC settings instead of adaptive ANC, or don't plan on making calls in noisy areas, then they're a nonissue anyway. The Nothing Ear 3A also include 32MB of on-device storage, allowing them to record up to two hours of a call or take an audio snapshot (Nothing's term) of up to one minute. When you then access the app, you can transfer the recordings onto your device. When beginning a call recording, a message plays to notify everyone. I can easily see the use of recording an important call to make sure you don't miss any information (although this can also easily be done through your phone), but I have yet to find a reason for the audio snapshot. It only records up to a minute of what you're listening to, not anything around you using the earbuds' microphones, at lower fidelity. It's unique to the Nothing 3A, but also gimmicky. I'm glad the Nothing Ear 3A returned to a price under $100 after the $179 Ear 3. Nothing is at its best when it's challenging what can be done for less - and I'm more forgiving of its minor flaws. While the sound wasn't my taste out of the box, the fact you can make meaningful adjustments and tune it to your preferences makes them more versatile than most earbuds at the same price. title: IT Services in Schaumburg, IL: What Local Businesses Actually Pay, Get, and Should Ask For
teaser: Schaumburg IT costs: Businesses should budget $100-$250 per user monthly, but must track separate fees for hardware & major projects.
summary: For businesses in Schaumburg, IL, understanding managed IT costs is crucial due to the area's dense mix of corporate offices, manufacturers, and healthcare providers. Comprehensive managed IT typically costs $100-$250 per user monthly. While service agreements cover essential operations (monitoring, help desk, security), they generally exclude major capital expenditures like hardware or large migrations. Beyond standard recurring support, businesses must factor in compliance needs (HIPAA, PCI-DSS) and potentially pay for professional labor ($150-$250/hour). The article advises separating recurring support from products and project work to ensure accurate budgeting.
author: Contributor
content: Schaumburg has nearly 5,000 businesses and more than 80,000 workers, making it one of the Chicago suburbs' largest employment centers. For companies evaluating outsourced IT, industry pricing guides put comprehensive managed IT at roughly $100-$250 per user per month , with the final cost driven by security requirements, support hours, infrastructure complexity, and compliance obligations. Why IT services matter more in Schaumburg than in most suburbs? Schaumburg's concentration of corporate offices, manufacturers, professional firms, warehouses, retailers, and healthcare organizations creates unusually high dependence on business IT. An outage can affect office users, cloud applications, warehouse systems, customer transactions, remote employees, and communications at the same time. The local economy combines the Woodfield business district, industrial properties near the I-90/IL-53 corridor, and companies connected to the broader O'Hare logistics belt. Zurich North America maintains its headquarters at 1299 Zurich Way beside I-90, while Motorola Solutions, whose global headquarters occupied Schaumburg for five decades before moving to Chicago in 2016, still maintains offices in the village. That business mix creates very different technical requirements within a relatively small geographic area. A 40-person law firm may depend primarily on Microsoft 365, document management, Microsoft Entra ID, secure remote access, and reliable backup. A 100-user warehouse may also depend on industrial Wi-Fi, scanners, shipping stations, shared workstations, VPN connections, printers, switches, and line-of-business applications. Manufacturing and logistics businesses along the I-90 corridor may operate outside a standard 9-to-5 schedule, making monitoring and after-hours incident handling more important. Accounting firms may face FTC Safeguards Rule requirements, healthcare practices may need HIPAA-related controls, and organizations accepting card payments may need to account for PCI-DSS requirements. For businesses with 10-200 employees, the practical question is therefore not simply whether an IT provider can fix computers. The provider needs to support the specific mix of endpoints, identity systems, cloud applications, networks, cybersecurity controls, backups, and compliance requirements that keeps the organization operating. What managed IT services include (and what they don't)? A comprehensive managed IT agreement normally covers recurring IT operations: monitoring, help desk support, endpoint security, patching, backup monitoring, and Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace administration. It usually does not mean that hardware, software licenses, major migrations, cabling, or every technology project is included in one flat monthly fee. Industry-standard managed services usually start with 24/7 remote monitoring and management . An RMM platform such as NinjaOne can monitor workstations, servers, system health, services, and patch status while allowing technicians to manage endpoints remotely. Help desk support typically covers recurring user issues such as password problems, Microsoft 365 errors, printer connections, application troubleshooting, workstation issues, and basic network access problems. Contracts described as "unlimited help desk" should still define which users, devices, applications, and hours are covered. Endpoint security should also be defined by function rather than by a generic statement such as "antivirus included." A modern security stack may use Bitdefender GravityZone for NGAV, EDR, XDR, or MDR capabilities; Microsoft Entra ID for identity, MFA, and SSO; SonicWall for firewall security; and Microsoft Intune for mobile-device and endpoint management. Patch management normally covers supported operating systems and selected third-party applications. The provider should be able to report patch compliance rather than simply state that automated updates are enabled. Backup services require similar precision. Platforms such as N-able Cove and Veeam can protect servers, endpoints, virtual machines, and cloud workloads, but the contract should specify what is backed up, how often backups run, how long data is retained, whether immutable copies exist, and how recovery is tested . Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace administration may include account provisioning, mailbox administration, security configuration, permissions, user changes, and licensing management. The recurring service fee does not necessarily include the actual Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace license cost. A useful managed-services proposal therefore separates recurring support from products and project work. That distinction makes two competing monthly prices much easier to compare. What's usually NOT in the flat fee? Managed IT flat fees usually exclude irregular or capital-intensive costs such as hardware, third-party software licenses, major migrations, office moves, structured cabling, and large infrastructure projects. After-hours project work and emergency support may also be charged separately depending on the provider's contract. Industry pricing guides commonly place out-of-scope professional-services labor around $150-$250 per hour . A Microsoft 365 migration, server replacement, firewall redesign, office relocation, or major network upgrade may therefore be quoted as a separate project. Onboarding is another common additional cost. Industry pricing guides often place onboarding at approximately 1-2 months of recurring service , although the amount depends on documentation quality, endpoint count, security remediation, network complexity, and the amount of tooling that must be deployed. Hardware is normally separate because a managed-service fee pays for ongoing operations rather than ownership of laptops, servers, switches, access points, and firewalls. Software licenses may also appear as separate line items even when the provider manages those applications. Before signing, ask the provider to place every service into one of four categories: included in the monthly fee, separately licensed, billable project work, or excluded . That classification is more useful than a vague promise of "all-inclusive IT." How much do IT services cost in Schaumburg? A Schaumburg business should generally budget about $100-$250 per user per month for comprehensive managed IT. Industry pricing guides commonly place total monthly spending for a typical 10-50-employee company around $1,500-$5,000, with cybersecurity, compliance, multiple sites, and complex infrastructure pushing costs higher. The pricing structure matters because two providers can quote similar monthly totals while including very different services. Pricing model Typical market range Best fit Per-user $100-$250/user/month Office-heavy businesses where employees use multiple devices and Microsoft 365 Per-device About $30-$150/device/month Businesses with shared PCs, warehouse stations, servers, kiosks, or specialized endpoints Tiered Varies by service tier and security scope Companies choosing predefined basic, standard, or security-focused packages Co-managed Varies substantially by retained internal IT responsibilities Businesses with internal IT staff outsourcing selected functions These figures are budgeting benchmarks rather than standardized tariffs. Per-user pricing is easier to compare across industry pricing guides, while per-device, tiered, and co-managed pricing depends more heavily on the number of supported systems and the exact division of responsibility. A 30-user accounting firm near Woodfield may pay more per user than another 30-person business if the agreement includes advanced email security, immutable backups, Microsoft Entra ID controls, endpoint detection and response, and FTC Safeguards Rule support. A 100-user warehouse near the I-90/IL-53 corridor may create a different cost structure. Its environment may include 100 employees but 160 managed devices, shared terminals, scanners, warehouse Wi-Fi, switches, firewalls, printers, shipping systems, and multiple operational shifts. The monthly figure therefore matters less than the scope behind it. A $125-per-user contract that excludes backup, security operations, after-hours incidents, and Microsoft 365 administration may cost more in practice than a $190-per-user agreement that includes those functions. Managed IT vs hiring in-house in the Chicago suburbs For many businesses below roughly 75 employees, outsourced IT can provide broader technical coverage than hiring one internal generalist. One in-house IT employee commonly represents roughly $80,000-$120,000 per year in salary and employment overhead while still providing only one person's working hours, experience, and availability. One internal administrator may be capable of handling Microsoft 365, endpoints, basic networking, user support, and vendors. That same person is unlikely to be equally specialized in cybersecurity, backup architecture, identity management, firewall engineering, compliance, cloud infrastructure, and disaster recovery. Availability creates another difference. One employee normally provides approximately 40 working hours per week , minus vacation, sick leave, meetings, and training. A managed-services provider can distribute tickets and escalations across multiple technicians and disciplines. In-house IT becomes easier to justify as organizations grow. Around 75+ employees , daily ticket volume, application ownership, vendor coordination, internal projects, and company-specific knowledge can create enough continuous work for dedicated internal staff. That does not make managed services unnecessary. A 100- or 150-employee company may employ an IT manager while outsourcing endpoint monitoring, EDR, backup operations, after-hours coverage, help desk overflow, or infrastructure engineering. The real comparison is therefore not simply "MSP versus employee." Businesses should compare the cost and capabilities of the entire IT operating model required to support their users. Fully managed vs co-managed: which model fits your business? Fully managed IT gives an outside provider primary responsibility for day-to-day IT operations, while co-managed IT supplements an existing internal IT team. The core difference is ownership and control: fully managed service replaces the internal IT function, while co-managed service divides responsibilities between internal staff and the provider. Responsibility Fully managed Co-managed Help desk Primarily MSP Internal team, MSP, or shared Monitoring and patching Primarily MSP Often MSP Cybersecurity operations Primarily MSP or security partner Shared or selectively outsourced Business-specific applications Shared with management/application vendors Often led internally IT strategy MSP with business leadership Internal IT leadership with MSP input Escalation engineering MSP MSP supports internal IT A 35-person construction company without an IT employee may be a strong fit for fully managed service. The provider can take primary responsibility for workstations, Microsoft 365, identity, mobile devices, backup, patching, endpoint security, firewall management, and user support. A 120-person manufacturer may have different requirements. An internal IT manager may understand ERP workflows, production systems, vendor relationships, and operational priorities better than an external provider ever could. Co-managed IT allows that internal manager to retain control while outsourcing selected functions such as 24/7 monitoring, EDR, backup infrastructure, patching, help desk overflow, or complex Microsoft 365 work. The division must be documented. A written responsibility matrix should identify who owns endpoint security, user onboarding, Microsoft 365 administration, firewall changes, backup testing, vendor management, procurement, projects, and incident response. Shared responsibility without named ownership creates gaps. During a ransomware incident or major outage, "we thought the other team handled it" is not an acceptable operating model. How to choose an IT services company in Schaumburg? 7 criteria A Schaumburg business should evaluate an IT provider across 7 areas: response performance, security architecture, contract terms, engineering depth, local service capability, compliance experience, and reporting. Each area should be supported by measurable service levels, named technologies, documented processes, or verifiable technical credentials. Criterion 1 - Measure response performance A provider that advertises 24/7 support should define what 24/7 actually means. Ask for average response times, SLA targets by severity, first-contact resolution rates, escalation procedures, and whether the first responder is an engineer or an intake agent. Criterion 2 - Require a named security stack A provider should be able to identify the technologies protecting endpoints, identities, networks, and backups. Examples include Bitdefender GravityZone for NGAV/EDR/XDR/MDR, SonicWall for firewall security, Microsoft Entra ID for MFA and SSO, and Microsoft Intune for device management. Criterion 3 - Compare contracts, not monthly prices A $140-per-user proposal and a $190-per-user proposal cannot be compared without examining scope. Review contract length, termination rights, onboarding fees, after-hours charges, project rates, hardware exclusions, licensing, SLA commitments, and documentation ownership. Criterion 4 - Verify engineering depth A 100-user organization should not depend on one technician for desktops, networks, cybersecurity, Microsoft 365, backups, and cloud systems. Certifications such as Microsoft and CompTIA credentials provide one verifiable signal, while a documented escalation structure provides another. Criterion 5 - Test local service capability A provider serving the Woodfield area, I-90/IL-53 corridor, and Schaumburg industrial districts should explain where technicians are based and how on-site work is dispatched. A local telephone number does not prove that a provider has practical field coverage in the northwest suburbs. Criterion 6 - Match compliance knowledge to your industry Healthcare practices may need HIPAA-related safeguards. Businesses handling payment-card data may need PCI-DSS controls. Financial organizations and certain accounting environments may fall under the FTC Safeguards Rule, while other organizations may map security controls against NIST CSF or SOX requirements. Criterion 7 - Require measurable reporting and planning Useful reports should quantify patch compliance, backup status, endpoint-security coverage, recurring ticket categories, asset lifecycle, and SLA performance. Strategic reviews should convert those metrics into a 12-36-month plan for hardware replacement, security improvements, cloud changes, and business growth. A worked example: how one local MSP checks these boxes? RIT Company provides one worked example of applying these criteria to a provider serving Schaumburg from nearby Addison , about 15 minutes away, with typical on-site travel of 20-25 minutes. Its managed IT services in Schaumburg include NinjaOne for 24/7 RMM, Bitdefender GravityZone NGAV with EDR/XDR/MDR, SonicWall, Cytracom ControlOne, Microsoft Entra ID, NinjaOne MDM and Intune, plus NinjaOne Backup, N-able Cove immutable cloud backups, and Veeam. The company reports an average help-desk response under 15 minutes, 70-80% first-contact resolution, a 99.9% uptime SLA measured monthly, month-to-month contracts, 80+ business clients, approximately 1,000 managed endpoints, and Microsoft- and CompTIA-certified engineers with more than 100 years of combined hands-on experience. Its stated compliance support covers HIPAA, PCI-DSS, SOX, the FTC Safeguards Rule, and NIST CSF, giving a prospective buyer concrete service, security, contractual, and compliance claims to verify during due diligence. Red flags when hiring IT support in Schaumburg The biggest warning signs are undefined service scope, vague cybersecurity claims, weak contract exit terms, no measurable response data, unclear backup ownership, and dependence on a single technician. Any provider that cannot explain these areas in writing creates operational and financial risk before the contract begins. Red flag What to ask "We handle cybersecurity" without named controls Which EDR, MFA, firewall, backup, and monitoring products are deployed? "Unlimited support" without defined exclusions Which requests become separately billable projects? Long contract with difficult termination What are the termination rights after month 6 or month 12? "24/7 support" without response metrics What are the response targets for critical and normal tickets? "Backup included" without recovery targets What are the RPO, RTO, retention, immutability, and restore-testing procedures? One technician without an escalation map Who handles security, networking, Microsoft 365, backup, and after-hours escalation? Credential ownership is another important warning sign. The client organization should retain appropriate ownership or administrative control over domains, Microsoft 365 tenants, cloud subscriptions, firewall configurations, backup data, and other business-critical systems. Documentation should also be portable. A company changing providers should be able to obtain an asset inventory, network documentation, licensing information, administrative credentials, vendor records, and relevant configuration details without a prolonged dispute. Ask how offboarding works before signing the original agreement. A responsible provider should be able to describe the process for transferring credentials, documentation, licenses, and operational knowledge to another provider. Security claims deserve the same scrutiny. Statements such as "100% protected," "unhackable," or "zero risk" are not credible cybersecurity commitments because no technical control eliminates all risk. FAQ 1. How much should managed IT services cost for a small business in Schaumburg? Industry pricing guides put comprehensive managed IT at roughly $100-$250 per user per month . A typical business with 10-50 employees may spend approximately $1,500-$5,000 monthly , with higher costs for 24/7 operations, advanced cybersecurity, compliance obligations, multiple locations, or complex network infrastructure. 2. What do managed IT services include? A typical full-service agreement includes 24/7 monitoring , remote help desk support, endpoint security, patch management, backup monitoring, and Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace administration. More comprehensive agreements may also cover firewalls, EDR/XDR, Microsoft Entra ID, Intune, cloud systems, and monthly or quarterly strategic reviews. 3. What is not included in managed services? Hardware, third-party software licenses, major migrations, office moves, structured cabling, and large infrastructure projects are commonly excluded from flat fees. Industry pricing guides often place separate project work around $150-$250 per hour , while onboarding can cost approximately 1-2 months of recurring service . 4. Is managed IT better than in-house IT? For many companies below approximately 75 employees , managed IT can provide broader technical coverage than one generalist. One internal IT employee may cost roughly $80,000-$120,000 annually with salary and employment overhead , while larger organizations may gain more value from combining internal IT leadership with an external provider. 5. What is the difference between managed and co-managed IT services? Fully managed IT makes the provider primarily responsible for help desk, monitoring, security, patching, and other recurring operations. Co-managed IT supplements internal staff. A 120-employee manufacturer , for example, may retain 1 internal IT manager while outsourcing 24/7 monitoring, EDR, backups, or escalation engineering. 6. How do I choose an IT service provider in Schaumburg? Evaluate at least 7 areas : response performance, security stack, contract terms, engineering depth, local service capability, compliance experience, and reporting. Ask for written SLAs, support exclusions, backup responsibilities, escalation procedures, and termination terms rather than choosing solely on the lowest monthly per-user price. Choosing an IT provider should start with a documented scope rather than a sales presentation. Compare 2-3 providers using the same employee count, locations, security requirements, support hours, compliance needs, and project assumptions, then review exclusions and SLAs line by line. A free 15-minute discovery call, including the one offered by RIT Company, is a low-risk way to evaluate whether a provider asks the right operational questions before recommending a contract. title: Remarkable’s refurbished bundle is an awesome deal that’s over $350 off
teaser: Score a Remarkable Paper Pro bundle for $449.99—a massive save of $368 off its standard $629 price!
summary:
The highly praised Remarkable Paper Pro is currently available at a significant discount via Woot. Normally priced at $629, the refurbished bundle—which includes the tablet, Marker Plus stylus, and Book Folio—is offered for $449.99 through July 31st, representing savings of $368 compared to purchasing new.

The 11.8-inch Paper Pro offers a realistic paper-like writing experience and features a rich color display designed for productivity (e.g., reviewing slide decks). author: Sheena Vasani
content: A lot of us here at The Verge are fans of Remarkable's digital note-taking tablets, and right now one of its higher-end options is much cheaper than usual. The Remarkable Paper Pro normally sells for $629 on its own, but Woot is currently offering a refurbished bundle for $449.99 through July 31st. It includes the tablet, a Marker Plus stylus, and a Book Folio, saving you $368 compared to buying new. The same refurbished bundle costs $649 from Remarkable and comes with a longer one-year warranty versus Woot's 90-day warranty. The 11.8-inch Paper Pro offers a paper-like writing experience, along with a rich color display. Unlike the monochromatic Paper Pure -Remarkable's latest tablet that retails for $399 - it features an adjustable front light, making it easier to read and keep working after the lights go down. It also supports (but does not include) the optional $229 Type Folio keyboard , allowing you to switch between handwriting and typing. Writing feels remarkably smooth - more so than similar devices from Boox, Kobo, and even Kindle Scribe models - while Remarkable's software lets you organize notebooks with folders and tags, write directly on PDFs, and quickly convert handwritten notes into typed text. Although it supports basic sketching features like layers and shading, an iPad Pro is a better tablet if you're serious about drawing. The Paper Pro's color display was made with productivity in mind, serving as a distraction-free experience for reviewing slide decks, marking up reports, editing text, and organizing color-coded notes.
